quote: Wie viele solche ganze Functionen im Modul sind nöthig, um alle Functionen $p$ ten Grades nach jeder $(p^{r})$ als Modul in Linearfactoren zer- legen zu können?
english: How many such integral functions in the modulus are necessary in order to be able to decompose all functions of degree $p$ into linear factors with respect to every $(p^{r})$ as modulus?
topic: The page ends a remark about Poincaré polygons whose opposite circular arcs are carried into each other, then poses questions on the irreducibility of x^{p^2}-px-p modulo (p^2, p) and on decomposing functions of degree p into linear factors modulo powers of p.

triage.modern_statement: This is my reading of a short note, not a sure one. It looks like a question about how many 'Galois imaginaries' (Kronecker/Schönemann double-modulus style) are needed for a splitting field. Fix a prime p. Suppose we keep adjoining roots of polynomials that are irreducible with respect to a modulus, such as x^{p^2}-px-p modulo (p^2, p). How many such adjunctions does it take before every polynomial of degree p factors into linear factors modulo p^r, for every r? In modern terms this probably means: over Q_p, find the compositum of the splitting fields of all degree-p polynomials, which is the same as the compositum of all extensions of Q_p of degree at most p. Is it a finite extension, and how many generators (or what degree) does it need?
triage.answered_by: No one answered this exact question as Hilbert wrote it. The tools needed came later. Hensel introduced p-adic numbers in 1897, which gives 'modulo p^r for every r' a precise meaning. Krasner's lemma then shows that a p-adic field has only finitely many extensions of a given degree. So the compositum of all degree-≤p extensions of Q_p is a finite extension, and finitely many adjunctions are enough. Krasner also gave formulas counting extensions of a given degree and discriminant. Pauli–Roblot and later authors made the enumeration algorithmic. I found no source that gives Hilbert's exact count (the minimal number of generators) for degree p.

evidence.claim: Kurt Hensel first described p-adic numbers in 1897. In hindsight, some of Kummer's earlier work can be read as implicitly using them.
A p-adic field has only finitely many extensions of a given finite degree, and Krasner gave formulas for the number of extensions of a given degree and discriminant.
Krasner's lemma implies that a local field has only finitely many extensions of a given degree and discriminant. There is ongoing work on enumerating these extensions.

triage.why: The note is brief, and how I map it onto modern terms is my own interpretation. The finiteness part is settled by standard p-adic theory: Hensel's p-adic numbers plus Krasner's finiteness result. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems, and I found no source that discusses this notebook question. Computing and enumerating local field extensions, for example in the Jones–Roberts and Pauli–Roblot line of work, is still active computational number theory. My searches turned up no source on Hilbert's specific question about the minimal number of adjunctions, so I can't say whether that exact count has been worked out.
